abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a theoretical framework for analyzing evolutionary algorithms in dynamic environments based on time-scale separation principles. Unlike conventional convergence analyses that assume stationary fitness landscapes, the proposed framework explicitly distinguishes between evolutionary dynamics time-scales and environmental change frequencies. By employing stochastic differential equation theory and measure transformation techniques, we establish rigorous bounds on tracking error that reveal fundamental relationships between selection pressure, mutation intensity, and environmental volatility. The framework introduces the concept of diversity buffering, demonstrating how population diversity functions as a stabilizing mechanism against environmental perturbations. We prove that parameter configurations exist beyond which system behavior undergoes phase transitions from tracking capability to evolutionary stagnation. This multi-time-scale perspective unifies previously fragmented approaches to dynamic evolutionary optimization, providing a coherent analytical paradigm from asymptotic convergence to rapid tracking. The theoretical contributions include necessary and sufficient conditions for consistent performance in non-stationary environments and explicit formulas connecting algorithm parameters with environmental characteristics. Empirical validation on benchmark dynamic optimization problems confirms the predictive power of the theoretical framework. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for understanding and designing evolutionary algorithms operating in real-world dynamic scenarios.

This paper substantially extends schema theory to address the computational complexity challenges inherent in genetic programming with variable-length representations. Traditional schema theory, developed primarily for fixed-length genetic algorithms, fails to adequately characterize the search dynamics of tree-based genetic programming where building block sizes are inherently flexible. We introduce the concept of variable-length schemata with adaptive building block granularity, enabling a more precise characterization of genetic programming dynamics. By developing probabilistic models of building block size distributions and their interaction with crossover operators, we derive tighter bounds on the exploration-exploitation tradeoff compared to existing theoretical analyses. The theoretical framework reveals fundamental relationships between population sizing, crossover probability, and the intrinsic scale structure of problems being evolved. These relationships provide guidance for designing genetic programming systems that can effectively balance convergence speed with solution diversity. Based on the theoretical analysis, we propose a building-block-aware crossover operator that preferentially recombines schemata with complementary building block sizes. Experimental validation on symbolic regression and Boolean function synthesis problems demonstrates that the proposed operator significantly improves genetic programming performance, validating the theoretical predictions. This work provides deeper theoretical understanding of genetic programming search dynamics and offers practical insights for operator design.

This paper proposes a novel hierarchical coevolutionary framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes multi-objective evolutionary optimization through problem decomposition and multi-level coordination. The framework decomposes complex multi-objective optimization problems into multiple cooperating evolutionary modules, each handling specific aspects of the problem structure. Unlike existing coevolutionary approaches that operate at a single scale, the proposed framework implements three-tier coordination: population-level evolution for Pareto approximation, archive-level evolution for diversity maintenance, and module-level evolution for adaptive operator selection. The framework introduces several key innovations: adaptive problem decomposition based on landscape analysis, dynamic module interaction mechanisms inspired by ecological speciation, and convergence-guaranteed coordination protocols. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis proving convergence to the Pareto front under realistic assumptions and characterize the computational complexity of the coordination mechanisms. The hierarchical architecture enables effective handling of problems with complex Pareto front geometries and strong epistatic relationships between decision variables. Comprehensive experimental evaluation on standard multi-objective benchmarks and real-world engineering design problems demonstrates that the proposed framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art multi-objective evolutionary algorithms. The framework represents a paradigm shift in multi-objective optimization, offering a scalable architecture for tackling increasingly complex optimization challenges.

This paper addresses the fundamental challenge of balancing convergence and diversity in large-scale multi-objective optimization through an innovative adaptive multi-archive management mechanism. Traditional archiving strategies struggle to maintain solution diversity while promoting convergence, particularly in high-dimensional objective spaces. The proposed system dynamically adjusts selection pressure based on real-time convergence assessment, enabling adaptive balancing between exploration and exploitation throughout the evolutionary process. The mechanism integrates hypervolume-based convergence estimation with density-sensitive archiving to maintain well-distributed solution sets along the Pareto front. A key innovation is the progressive selection pressure adjustment strategy, which gradually intensifies convergence pressure as the population approaches the Pareto front. The proposed archiving mechanism is theoretically grounded in convergence analysis and computationally lightweight for practical implementation. Extensive experimental evaluation on standard multi-objective benchmarks including problems with up to 15 objectives demonstrates substantial improvements over state-of-the-art archiving strategies. The proposed mechanism achieves superior performance across multiple performance indicators, particularly in convergence metrics while maintaining competitive diversity preservation. The adaptive archiving system provides a principled approach to addressing the scalability challenges in multi-objective evolutionary optimization.
